strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel dataset type—large-scale spatial multigraphs—filling a real gap in graph learning benchmarks where prior work either used simple graphs or collapsed multi-edges into single weighted edges.

Strong physics grounding: the construction is rigorously tied to non-Hermitian band theory and non-Bloch band theory, with detailed mathematical exposition (spectral potential, DOS, GBZ) in the appendix.

Large scale and class diversity (11.6M static + 5.1M dynamic graphs across 1401 classes) substantially exceeds existing graph-classification datasets in class diversity, as shown in comparison figures/tables.

Poly2Graph pipeline is a valuable standalone contribution: open-source, well-documented (extensive tutorial in appendix F), with reported large speed/memory improvements over prior non-automated approaches, enabling extensibility beyond the released dataset.
Comprehensive comparison with dozens of existing benchmark datasets (Table A3) situates the contribution clearly relative to prior work across many domains.
The paper provides multiple dataset variants (one-band/two-band/three-band/topology/temporal) tailored to different research needs and difficulty levels, increasing usability.

Interesting theoretical extension (Section 6, Appendix E) connecting spectral graphs to arbitrary matrices/polynomials via Toeplitz decomposition, suggesting broader relevance beyond condensed matter physics.
weaknesses: Benchmarking is incomplete and admittedly minimal: only 3 of 6 dataset variants (the smaller ones) are evaluated, with the flagship HSG-12M, HSG-three-band, and T-HSG-5M explicitly left unbenchmarked due to "limited resources," undermining the claim that the paper establishes meaningful baselines for its own large-scale resource.

Only vanilla, off-the-shelf GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE) with generic global-sum pooling are tested; no multi-edge-aware or geometry-aware architectures are evaluated, despite the paper's central claim that the dataset requires such methods—leaving the core motivating premise empirically unverified.

Reported baseline performance is very poor and highly variable (e.g., GIN achieves ~0.2% top-1 accuracy on HSG-topology, near-random for several models), which could reflect either a genuinely hard/interesting task or poorly suited featurization/training setup (only 5 epochs, minimal hyperparameter tuning); the paper does not sufficiently disambiguate these possibilities.

Average graph size is very small (mean ~13.8 nodes, ~28.9 edges per graph), which is atypical for a benchmark motivated by "rich multi-edge geometry"; it's unclear whether such small graphs truly necessitate new geometry-aware, multigraph-specific learning techniques versus simpler featurization tricks.

The class definition and sampling scheme (based on systematic enumeration of polynomial coefficient combinations) may produce many classes with limited practical/scientific distinctiveness; the paper does not analyze inter-class similarity or verify that classification difficulty stems from meaningful physical differences rather than an artifact of the sampling procedure.

The "universal algebra-to-graph" claims (Section 6, Appendix E) are largely conceptual/speculative, resting on an existence theorem (matrix decomposition into Toeplitz factors) without any empirical demonstration or use case validating practical utility for vectors/matrices outside the crystal Hamiltonian setting.

Downstream scientific utility is asserted (accelerating materials discovery, quantum sensing, etc.) but not demonstrated with any concrete physics task or property-prediction experiment connecting graph structure to actual physical observables.

Some benchmarking results have very large relative variance (e.g., GIN/GAT on HSG-two-band and topology), and no statistical significance testing or deeper error analysis is provided to contextualize these fluctuations.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel dataset domain -- spatial multigraphs derived from non-Hermitian quantum spectral theory -- which fills an acknowledged gap, as no large-scale multigraph or spatial multigraph benchmark previously existed.

The Poly2Graph pipeline is a solid engineering contribution: it automates an otherwise manual process, is open-sourced with MIT license, provides extensive documentation/tutorials, and reports substantial speed/memory improvements over prior tools.

Extensive appendix material (mathematical background, algorithm details, dataset comparison tables, package tutorial) supports reproducibility and gives the work a thorough, well-documented presentation.

The paper situates the contribution carefully against a large body of related work on multigraphs and spatial graphs, with a comprehensive comparison table (Table A3) against dozens of existing benchmarks.

The conceptual link between spectral graphs and general algebraic objects (polynomials, vectors, matrices via Toeplitz decomposition) is an interesting, potentially generative idea for future work, even if underdeveloped here.
weaknesses: The benchmarking is substantially incomplete: the authors explicitly state that the three largest and most emphasized dataset variants (HSG-three-band, the flagship HSG-12M itself, and T-HSG-5M) were never benchmarked 'due to limited resources.' This undermines the central claim that the dataset enables large-scale geometry-aware learning challenges, since no experiments actually probe behavior at the claimed 12M-graph scale.

Baselines are minimal and generic (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE with only 4 layers, 5 training epochs, no hyperparameter search), so the reported numbers are not convincing evidence of the described 'new challenges' -- they mostly show that under-trained models perform poorly, which is unsurprising and not very informative.

Despite motivating the dataset around the importance of multi-edge geometry, no ablation or control experiment isolates the contribution of geometric edge features versus pure topology (e.g., comparing models with/without coordinate-based edge features). It is therefore unclear whether the central claimed novelty (geometry-aware multigraph learning) is actually demonstrated to matter.

No comparison against existing multigraph-specific learning methods (the paper cites relevant work, e.g. refs on multigraph/directed-multigraph GNNs, but does not benchmark them), despite the paper's claim that this is the first large-scale testbed for such methods.

The 1401 'classes' are generated by a fixed combinatorial sampling scheme over polynomial coefficients rather than arising from naturally diverse phenomena, raising questions about whether the touted 'exceptional class diversity' reflects meaningful physical diversity or is largely an artifact of the synthetic construction procedure.

The claims in Section 6 (any matrix/vector/polynomial admits a spectral-graph fingerprint) are asserted conceptually via a decomposition argument but are not empirically validated or shown to be useful for any concrete downstream task, making this contribution feel speculative rather than substantiated.

The practical scientific utility of the dataset is not demonstrated beyond classification into (synthetically defined) characteristic-polynomial classes; there is no evaluation on physically meaningful downstream tasks (e.g., predicting topological invariants, phase classification, or material design outcomes) that would justify the stated relevance to 'rational design of materials' or 'accelerating discovery of exotic phases.'

Quality assurance of Poly2Graph is limited to visual inspection of 'hundreds' of characteristic polynomials; no quantitative validation against exact diagonalization (e.g., error rates, fragmentation statistics across the full dataset) is reported, despite acknowledged failure modes (component fragmentation) that could affect a non-trivial fraction of the released graphs.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel dataset type—large-scale spatial multigraphs—filling a clear and previously unaddressed gap in graph representation learning benchmarks (no prior large-scale multigraph or spatial multigraph dataset existed).

Strong physics grounding: the dataset is derived from rigorous non-Hermitian/non-Bloch band theory, giving each graph class a precise physical meaning (characteristic polynomial classes tied to 1D crystal Hamiltonians), which adds scientific value beyond a synthetic benchmark.

Poly2Graph is a substantial engineering contribution: reported 10^6x speedup and 20-40x memory reduction over prior methods via a custom companion-matrix root solver, adaptive two-stage resolution scheme, and GPU/TPU-agnostic backend, enabling dataset construction that was previously computationally infeasible.

Very thorough documentation and reproducibility support: detailed appendices covering mathematical background, algorithmic pipeline (with pseudocode), dataset comparison tables against ~50 existing datasets, and an extensive open-source tutorial with code examples.

Thoughtful dataset design offering multiple scale/complexity variants (one/two/three-band, topology-only, temporal) tailored to different research needs, plus a large first-of-its-kind temporal spatial multigraph collection (T-HSG-5M).

Benchmarking with four standard GNN architectures across multiple metrics (Top-1/Top-10 accuracy, Macro-F1) provides a reasonable initial baseline and clearly demonstrates that existing methods struggle with multi-edge geometry and class imbalance, motivating future methodological work.

Interesting theoretical extension (Section 6) connecting spectral graphs to a more general "algebra-as-graph" perspective (polynomials, vectors, matrices via Toeplitz decomposition), broadening potential relevance beyond condensed matter physics.
weaknesses: Benchmarking is incomplete relative to the dataset's advertised scale: the largest and most emphasized variants (HSG-three-band, the full HSG-12M, and T-HSG-5M) are not benchmarked at all due to stated resource constraints, leaving the core 12M-graph contribution empirically untested.

Training budget for baselines is very short (5 epochs, no early stopping, minimal hyperparameter tuning), so the reported GNN results may not reflect achievable performance, weakening the evidentiary value of the benchmark as currently presented.

No geometry-aware or multi-edge-aware models are proposed or evaluated; only standard node-coordinate GNNs are tested with a fairly simple featurization (fixed equidistant edge point sampling), which does not exploit the dataset's central selling point (continuous edge geometry) and leaves the paper's central methodological challenge unaddressed even preliminarily.

The "universal relevance" claims in Section 6 (any polynomial/vector/matrix admits a spectral-graph fingerprint via Toeplitz decomposition) are asserted without any empirical demonstration, and the underlying decomposition is explicitly non-unique, making the practical utility of this claim unclear.

Quality assurance of Poly2Graph is limited to visual inspection on "hundreds" of polynomials rather than systematic quantitative validation against exact diagonalization across the sampled polynomial space actually used to build HSG-12M.

The component fragmentation artifact (mentioned as an intrinsic limitation) is acknowledged but not quantified—no statistics are given on what fraction of the 12M/5M graphs are affected, which is important given it directly impacts label/graph quality.

The class taxonomy (1401 characteristic-polynomial classes) arises from a systematic combinatorial enumeration procedure; it is not clear how much of the apparent "exceptional class diversity" reflects genuinely distinct physical/topological structure versus combinatorial artifacts of the sampling scheme.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel resource: the first large-scale spatial multigraph dataset (11.6M static + 5.1M temporal graphs across 1401 classes), filling a real gap since virtually all existing graph-classification benchmarks collapse multi-edges into simple graphs.

Poly2Graph pipeline is a substantial engineering contribution, combining non-Bloch band theory, algebraic root-finding via companion matrices, and adaptive-resolution image processing to achieve a claimed ~10^5x speedup over prior manual/semi-manual methods, making large-scale generation feasible.

Extensive and well-organized comparison against 45 existing graph datasets (Table A4) convincingly situates the contribution relative to prior work in scale, class diversity, spatial richness, and multiplicity.

Thorough benchmarking of 8 popular GNN architectures with multiple metrics (Accuracy, Macro-F1, Top-k, memory, throughput) and multiple dataset variants (one/two/three-band, topology, temporal), with reasonably controlled comparisons (matched parameter counts, fixed budgets) and low seed variance.

Rich supplementary material: detailed mathematical background connecting non-Hermitian physics to graph theory, a released open-source package with tutorials, and a broader vision connecting the method to algebra-to-graph mappings (Toeplitz decomposition of arbitrary matrices).

Physically motivated downstream task framing (inverse design via Top-k retrieval of Hamiltonian families) gives the classification benchmark some scientific grounding rather than being an arbitrary ML task.
weaknesses: The benchmarking is purely a survey of existing off-the-shelf GNNs with a simplified, fixed-size, direction-agnostic edge featurization (length, straight-line distance, midpoint, average potential/DOS); this actually discards most of the continuous multi-edge geometry that the paper emphasizes as the key novel challenge, so the benchmark does not really test "geometry-aware" or "spatial multigraph" learning as advertised—no new method or architecture is proposed to address the stated gap.

Reported Top-1 accuracies remain modest (e.g., ~0.55 best on HSG-12M) and the paper offers no deeper analysis of failure modes beyond generic statements; the paper leaves essentially all substantive modeling contributions as "future work," reducing its novelty as an ML methods paper (though this may be acceptable for a pure dataset/benchmark track).

The classification task itself (predicting the characteristic-polynomial/hopping-pattern class from the spectral graph) is defined by the same synthetic generative process used to create the dataset; its practical significance for real materials discovery or inverse design is asserted but not empirically demonstrated (e.g., no case study connecting predictions back to a physically realized material or design).

Component fragmentation (edges/nodes spuriously disconnected due to low DOS near junctions) is an acknowledged and non-trivial data-quality issue, particularly for larger hopping ranges/band counts, potentially affecting label/topology fidelity for a nontrivial fraction of the dataset (e.g., HSG-three-band, HSG-12M).

High Top-10 accuracy despite low Top-1 could partly reflect redundancy/near-duplication among the 1401 classes (many classes may yield visually/geometrically similar graphs) rather than strong ranking ability of the models; this is not analyzed or ruled out.

The fixed training budget (100 epochs / 1000 steps) and equalized-parameter protocol, while aiding fairness, may not reflect each architecture's true capacity, and the paper itself acknowledges this could bias conclusions like "GraphSAGE excels," limiting the reliability of comparative claims among GNNs.

The broader "universal algebra-to-graph" claims (Section 5, Appendix F) connecting arbitrary matrices/vectors/polynomials to spectral graphs via Toeplitz decomposition are conceptually interesting but remain speculative/theoretical without any empirical demonstration or use case within the paper.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and physically well-grounded data source (non-Hermitian spectral graphs) that is, to the authors' knowledge, the first large-scale spatial multigraph dataset for graph-level ML tasks, filling a real gap in existing graph-learning benchmarks that overwhelmingly use simple graphs.

Poly2Graph pipeline is technically well engineered: it combines non-Bloch band theory, an efficient Frobenius-companion-matrix root solver, and a two-stage adaptive-resolution image pipeline, yielding a claimed 10^5x speedup over the best prior (non-automated) code, which is a meaningful systems contribution enabling the dataset's scale.

The paper is extremely thorough in its documentation: extensive appendices cover mathematical background (non-Bloch theory, GBZ, characteristic polynomial classes), algorithmic details, a 45-dataset comparison table, and a full package tutorial, supporting reproducibility.

The benchmarking is reasonably comprehensive (8 GNN baselines, multiple metrics including Top-k, macro-F1, throughput, and memory), and the empirical findings (edge-awareness matters, degradation with task difficulty, high Top-10 vs moderate Top-1) are sensibly interpreted and physically motivated via an inverse-design framing.

The 'universality' discussion (Toeplitz decomposition linking arbitrary matrices/polynomials/vectors to spectral graph multisets) is a conceptually interesting extension that broadens potential impact beyond the immediate physics domain.
weaknesses: The core claimed novelty of 'spatial multigraph' is undercut by the reference featurization actually used for benchmarking: edges are reduced to a fixed-size, direction-ignorant 6-dimensional summary (length, straight-line distance, midpoint, avg potential/DOS), discarding the continuous curve geometry that is touted as the paper's central contribution; thus the presented benchmark does not actually test learning on genuine spatial multi-edges, somewhat contradicting the framing in the abstract/intro.

The 1401 'classes' are generated by a fairly mechanical combinatorial sampling scheme over monomial supports of low-hopping-range, low-band polynomials (one-, two-, three-band, hopping range 4-6) with fixed coefficient grids; this raises questions about real diversity/difficulty versus a combinatorial artifact of the construction (e.g., many classes may be near-degenerate or trivially distinguishable by non-geometric cues like degree bounds), which is not analyzed.

No new learning method is proposed for spatial multigraphs despite this being advertised as a key gap; the 'benchmark' with 8 off-the-shelf GNNs under a fairly restrictive, arbitrarily fixed training budget (max_epochs=100, max_steps=1000) and parameter-matching is a relatively thin empirical contribution for a dataset paper, and conclusions like 'GraphSAGE excels' are only valid within this narrow, somewhat arbitrary budget — the authors admit this themselves but do not attempt a budget ablation.

Physical/scientific validation is weak: 'quality assurance' is limited to visual inspection on 'hundreds' of polynomials against exact diagonalization, with no quantitative error metrics, no systematic validation across the actual 1401-class dataset, and known failure modes (component fragmentation) are acknowledged but not quantified in terms of how many graphs in HSG-12M are affected.

The practical downstream utility claims (materials inverse design, accelerating discovery of exotic phases) are speculative and not substantiated by any case study connecting predicted ChP classes back to realizable material parameters or experimental validation; the benchmark task itself (ChP-class classification) is a proxy whose relationship to real inverse materials design is asserted but not demonstrated.

Dataset variants (HSG-one/two/three-band, topology, T-HSG-5M, HSG-12M) are all derived from the same underlying generative scheme and parameter grid, so overlap/redundancy across 'variants' is high; presenting six variants somewhat inflates the apparent breadth of contribution without six genuinely distinct resources.

Scale claims (12M graphs, 177TB) are impressive on paper but each graph is fairly small (avg ~13.8 nodes, ~28.9 edges per Table A4), and given the templated construction, the information content/diversity per graph may be considerably lower than suggested by sheer graph count, which is not addressed quantitatively (e.g., no diversity/entropy analysis of graph topologies beyond isomorphism counts in the topology variant).

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated data domain (non-Hermitian crystal spectral graphs) grounded in solid physical/mathematical theory (non-Bloch band theory, generalized Brillouin zone, spectral potential/Ronkin function), with the appendix providing a thorough, rigorous derivation chain from Hamiltonian to spectral graph.

The Poly2Graph pipeline is a real engineering contribution: replacing brute-force root finding with a Frobenius companion-matrix formulation plus batched/parallel GPU eigensolvers and a two-stage adaptive-resolution scheme yields a claimed 10^5x speedup over prior manual/semi-manual approaches, which is what makes large-scale dataset construction feasible at all.

HSG-12M is large in both graph count (11.6M static + 5.1M temporal) and class diversity (1401 characteristic-polynomial classes), and the paper provides an extensive (45-dataset) comparison table substantiating the claim that it is the first large-scale spatial multigraph benchmark, filling a real gap since most existing graph datasets collapse multi-edges or ignore edge geometry.

Good reproducibility posture: open-source MIT-licensed code, CC-BY dataset release via Dataverse, detailed tutorials/appendices (30+ pages) covering API usage, hyperparameters, and training configurations for all 8 baseline GNNs.

The benchmarking, while not methodologically novel, is reasonably comprehensive (8 GNN baselines, multiple metrics including Top-k/macro-F1, memory/throughput reporting, parameter-matched comparisons) and yields interpretable findings (e.g., edge-aware GINE >> edge-agnostic GIN, high Top-10 despite modest Top-1, attention models underperforming under multi-edge density).

The generalization to "algebra-as-graph" (via Toeplitz decomposition, universality of spectral graphs for polynomials/vectors/matrices) is a nice conceptual bonus that broadens potential impact beyond the immediate physics application.
weaknesses: The paper argues that collapsing multi-edge geometry loses essential information, yet its own reference PyG featurization for benchmarking uses fixed-size, direction-agnostic scalar edge summaries (length, midpoint, avg potential/DOS) rather than the full curve geometry — so the actual benchmarked task does not really test learning over the rich spatial multigraph structure the paper emphasizes as its core novelty; no new architecture is proposed to actually consume the continuous edge geometry.

Dataset quality validation is fairly weak for a resource of this scale: the pipeline was reportedly checked by "visually inspecting hundreds of characteristic polynomials" against exact diagonalization, with no systematic, quantitative error-rate estimate across the 11.6M generated graphs; the acknowledged "component fragmentation" failure mode (spurious disconnection of branches at low-DOS junctions, especially for high-band/long-range hopping) is not quantified in terms of how many classes/graphs in HSG-12M are affected.

Benchmark baselines are limited to fairly standard/older GNNs (GCN, GAT(v2), GIN(E), MF, CGCNN, SAGE); no geometry-aware or equivariant architectures (e.g., E(n)-GNNs, edge-sequence/transformer models) are tested despite the dataset's explicitly spatial/multigraph nature, so the paper does not demonstrate that any existing method can meaningfully exploit the continuous geometric signal it argues is essential.

Top-1 accuracy remains low on the harder splits (e.g., ~35–55% on HSG-12M) and macro-F1 tracks similarly; while the paper frames this as motivation for future work, it leaves open whether the classification task as defined (1401 characteristic-polynomial classes from a systematic combinatorial sampling) is a well-posed or practically meaningful ML challenge versus an artifact of the enumeration procedure.

The physical/practical utility of the benchmark for actual inverse materials design is largely aspirational (discussed qualitatively in Section 5) without any concrete case study connecting predicted characteristic-polynomial classes back to realizable material designs or experimental validation.

Some superlative claims ("first large-scale spatial multigraph dataset," "universal topological fingerprints") are strong and rely on comprehensive but ultimately incomplete literature comparisons; the Toeplitz-decomposition "universality" argument in Section 5/Appendix F is more of a conceptual sketch than a rigorously developed or empirically demonstrated capability.
